## 2.2 Henze-Zirkler Test For Multivariate Normality 
:::{.center}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{H}_0 :& 
\text{ The data follow a multivariate normal distribution},
\\
\mathcal{H}_1 :& 
\text{ The data do not follow a multivariate normal distribution}.
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

## 2.3 Transformations

## 2.3 QQ plot and Henze-Zirkler Test for Multivariate Normality

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

#log transform data

logIngots <- log(as.matrix(Ingots_F_no[-1,-1]))
#print(logIngots)

knitr::kable(logIngots,
             caption = "Log Transformed Data",
             digits = 2,
             format = "pipe")

```

```{r echo = FALSE}
#taking the log.

qqnorm(logIngots, col = "#648FFF", main = "Normal QQ-Plot for the log-Transformed Data",
       sub = "All Elements")
qqline(logIngots, col = "#DC267F")

```

The QQ-plot of the log transformed data roughly followed the theoretical line (in red), this is evidence that the normality assumption may hold. The tails are relatively long and flat, indicating that there may be some extreme outliers. There are several steps in the upper and lower tails, which alone is not necessarily a departure from normality, and may be explained by the zero values returned for some Sample's variables after the log transformation.

The observed zero-values for (PUT SAMPLES NUMBERS IN HERE) in (TABLE) in variables(HERE), which while not a large quantity of the samples, still provided some concern as log(0) is undefined and can influence non-normality in multivariate data. The negative values are not an issue because we will be using metrics which are calculated from coordinate distances for clustering, and can handle negative values.

We chose to combat the zero values by standardising the data set using log($\mathcal{x}$ + 1)}, where $\mathcal{x}$ is our data. This, coupled with a Henze-Zirkler test, established if there is preliminary evidence for multivariate normality.

```{r echo = FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

#log transform data

logIngots1 <- log(as.matrix(Ingots_F_no[-1,-1] + 1))

#print(logIngots1)

knitr::kable(logIngots1,
             caption = "Log Transformed Data",
             format = "pipe")

#taking the log.

qqnorm(logIngots1, col = "#648FFF", main = "Normal QQ- Plot of the log-transformed data (all elements)")
qqline(logIngots1, col = "#DC267F")


HZoriginal <- mvn(data = logIngots1, mvn_test = "hz")

hz_table <- HZoriginal$multivariate_normality

knitr::kable(
  hz_table,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Henze-Zirkler Test For Multivariate Normality"
)
```

As you can see in table 2, our values are now all non-zero.

The normal QQ-plot looks less normal after standardisation, with the length of the tails being accentuated and continuing presence of stepped data.

The Henze-Zirkler test stipulates


This generated a p-value=0.069, suggesting that there is insufficient evidence to reject that the data follow a multivariate normal distribution. However, the QQ-plot shows enough \<flat tails, step, steep, etc\> that further testing is warranted before determining if multivariate normality is likely.

Given the uncertainty of multivariate normality and the presence of outliers, further data manipulation by Medioid Absolute Deviation was determined to be the next best step towards multivariate analysis.

## 2.3 MAD

MAD was used because it is a robust, outlier-resistant, measure of variability. The log transformation somewhat fixed the skew and pulled the outliers in, but did not eliminate their mathematical influence.

```{r transformations-mad, echo=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

#Calculate medians and MAD for each column:
median <- apply(logIngots1[,-1], 2, median)
mad <- apply(logIngots1[,-1], 2, mad)


#print(median/mad)
#mad

med_mad_table <- data.frame(
  Median = median,
  Mad = mad,
  Median_over_Mad = median/mad
)

knitr::kable(med_mad_table,
             caption = "Median / MAD",
             digits = 2,
             format = "pipe")

```

From {TABLE NUMBER} we observed some massive deviations, as expected.

Next the robust Z score was used to identify outliers that were candidates for removal. For our cutoff, we went with @Leys2013-cr recommendation, who argued that the MAD is the most robust scale measure under contamination and recommend a median plus or minus 2.5 time MAD rule for outlier detection.

```{r outliers, echo=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

#Compute the robust z-scores:
z <- scale(logIngots1[,-1], center = median, scale = mad)

#Flag observations where any variable exceeds the threshold
outliers <- apply(abs(z) > 2.5, 1, any)

#list(outliers)

# View the rows flagged as outliers
invisible(summary(logIngots1[outliers,]))

#The QQ plot of the mad transformed data:

qqnorm((z), col="#785EF0", main = "Normal QQ-Plot of 
       MAD-Transformed data")
qqline((z), col="red")

num_cols <- sapply(logIngots1, is.numeric)
z_scores <- as.data.frame(scale(logIngots1[, ]))

#summary(z_scores)

ol <- logIngots1[rowSums(abs(z_scores) > 4) > 0, ] #ALICE STUFF

print(ol) # ALICE STUFF

Ingots_clean <- logIngots1[rowSums(abs(z_scores) > 2.5) == 0, ]

#summary(Ingots_clean)

#New boxplot:

df <- as.data.frame(Ingots_clean)

Ingots_clean_long <- df[,-1] |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Elements",
    values_to = "Concentrations")



ggplot(Ingots_clean_long, aes(x= Elements, y= Concentrations)) +
  geom_boxplot(notch = FALSE, fill ="#40B0A6") +
  theme_minimal()+
  labs(title = "Boxplot of MAD Transformation With Outliers Removed")


#still getting negative values (even with elevated magnitude cutoff) in here so 
#log transforming may not be appropriate.

logIngotsClean <- invisible(log(as.matrix(Ingots_clean[-1,-1])))
invisible(summary(logIngotsClean))

#head(logIngotsClean)


#making the dataframe numeric so it can be manipulated.

num_vars <- sapply(Ingots_clean, is.numeric)

```

The QQ plot shows very skewed data which we would expected...

What is after we have "cleaned" up the outliers our \|z\| \> 3 rule removes samples 13, 25, and 38 which is exactly the sample ingots that Caponetti et al. set aside as their G4 group.

{should probably explain why cutting out 11 samples will be good for the rest of our analysis, something along the line of outliers, terrible samples and low sample quality}.

**2.4 Multivariate normal distribution**

What tests did we use? Henze Zirkler

Why did we use those tests?

```{R Henze Zirkler, echo=FALSE, warning = FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

#HZ test on OG data, which also rejects null.

HZoriginal <- mvn(data = Ingots_F_no, mvn_test = "hz")
cat("Henze_Zirkler Test Results:\n")
print(HZoriginal$multivariate_normality)

#Henze-Zirkler test on cleaned data?
#Non-negative functional distance that measures between two distribution functions. If data
#is MVN, the test statistic HZ is approximately lognormally distributed. It calculates mean,
#variance, and smoothness parameter. Mean and variance are then log-normalised and p-value
#is estimated.
#@MISC{noauthor_undated-de,
#  howpublished = "\url{https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/MVN/versions/5.8/topics/hzTest}",
#  note         = "Accessed: 2026-9-15"
#}

HZ <- mvn(data = Ingots_clean, mvn_test = "hz")

cat("Henze_Zirkler Test Results:\n")
print(HZ$multivariate_normality)
```

Due to our Henze Zirkler test for both the un-transformed data (p-value \<0.001) and the transformed data (p-value 0.046) we can safety reject the null hypotheses and conclude that the data regardless if it is transformed or not does not follow a multivariate normal distribution.

As our data isn't multivariate it isn't appropriate to perform a mahalanobis distance. {could potentially do need to research tho}

**2.5 Correlation plots before and after**

![Correlation matrix of Raw Data](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luke8471/STAT394-GROUP-3/main/Figures/correlation_matrix.png)

![Correlation matrix of log-Transformed Data](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luke8471/STAT394-GROUP-3/main/Figures/correlation_matrix_log.png)

Seeing a lot more correlation in the data with the massive outliers removed. Correlation plot some things to highlight; is that the strong positive association between V and Cr is also strongly positively association in the data with the outlying samples removes.. The transformed data also clearly shows a strong positive association for Bi and Ag which the un-transformed data doesn't show as significantly. the negative association between Zn and Te becomes more stronger in the transformed data.

The transformation didn't just strength some of the associations it also happened to reverse the sign for several of the relationships, Bi and Mn was one the raw data had a positive association but the transformed data turned it into a negative association similar with the relation ships between Sb and Sn as well as Rb and Te. It went the other direction (negative to positive) for As and Co. This is a positive sign that the robustness of the transformation, i.e removing some of the outliers demonstrates their influence on the raw data.

Given the uncertainty about multivariate normality, a linear data analysis was chosen over a primary component analysis.
